Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
Nothing good can happen to me anymore

vignette:
Omar, a 26-year-old editor, presented for treatment six months after an incident involving a wrongful police stop. Until that night, he had described his life as structured and meaningful, built around his marriage and a career he found fulfilling. Now, he feels adrift in a world that has become a landscape of hidden threats. The event occurred as he and his wife were walking home from dinner. Responding to a robbery report with a vague description, two officers cornered them. A female officer, in particular, was aggressive, her voice sharp as she ordered him face-down on the damp, cold pavement. He remembers the specific chill of the concrete against his cheek, the smell of rain on the asphalt mixed with the officer's cloying floral perfume, and the wrenching pain in his shoulders as his hands were cuffed behind him. Though he was released within minutes once they realized their mistake, the public humiliation and terror of the event fractured his sense of safety.

In the months since, the memory of that night has refused to stay in the past. When it returns, it is not just an image but a full sensory replay. He is suddenly overwhelmed by a profound and staggering grief for the man he was before that night, a man who felt safe in his own neighborhood. His body involuntarily reenacts the trauma; he feels his shoulders ache and twist as if his arms are still pinned behind his back. The phantom smell of wet concrete can fill his nostrils without warning. Because these fragments of the trauma could ambush him at any moment, he found himself constantly on guard, scanning his environment for any hint of a similar smell, a particular temperature, or the presence of a woman who might resemble the officer. These intrusive sensory fragments serve as constant, visceral proof of his deepest fears about himself. Each time his body betrays him with these reenactments, the thought crystallizes: his reactions show that he is a lousy coper, permanently broken by the experience. This conviction, in turn, makes him more vigilant, constantly scanning for anything that might bring the memory back.

This hypervigilance is fueled by his negative beliefs about himself and the world. Because he is certain that nothing good can happen to him anymore, his mind is primed for danger. He finds himself constantly monitoring the temperature of surfaces, his own internal state, and the presence of others. This focus makes him exquisitely sensitive to his triggers. A moment of feeling slightly detached or unreal, once a passing sensation, is now a terrifying alarm bell signaling that a full-blown memory is imminent. Being alone with a woman he doesn’t know well, particularly at his editing job when meeting with new authors, invokes the specific helplessness he felt under the gaze of the female officer. When a new writer came to his office last month, the simple act of closing the door behind her sent a wave of panic through him. This immediate, powerful reaction only served to confirm his belief that he is fundamentally incapable of handling life, which then pulls the memories of the event, with all their attendant grief and physical sensations, closer to the surface.

This vicious cycle has steadily dismantled his life. At work, he has started making excuses to avoid one-on-one meetings with female colleagues, insisting a junior editor sit in or handling all correspondence over email, a change in behavior that has not gone unnoticed by his manager. The appraisal that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore has drained the color from everything he once enjoyed, including his marriage. He feels a profound sense of guilt that being in a room alone with a woman can be a trigger, a confusing and shameful reality he has been unable to explain to his wife, creating a painful distance between them. The world feels unsafe, and he feels utterly unequipped to navigate it. It was after he found himself frozen in his own kitchen, unable to move for several minutes because his hand had brushed against the cold metal of the refrigerator, that his wife insisted he seek help. Omar came to therapy hoping to quiet the memories, but what he fears most is that his belief is true: that he is a lousy coper, and that nothing good can ever happen to him again.

violations.explanation: The vignette is missing the causal relationship where the trauma memory leads to increased vigilance or sensitivity to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette is missing the causal relationship where the trauma memory leads to increased vigilance or sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
